judge: Claude Opus 5.5, the EU Code of Practice (Safety & Security) source expert (a fork of expert-eu-cop-2025-safety-security), judging blind: no source-search output and no other judge's file seen before this file was written
read: whole, in order, at least 150 words per unit, with a written reflection after each (124 units; experts/eu-cop-2025-safety-security/reading/ on branch expert/eu-cop-2025-safety-security); then the AI Act provisions it builds on, a PDF check, and the Chairs' statement

hazard.quote: 'systemic risk source' | a factor which alone or in combination with other factors might give rise to systemic risk
hazard.note: The Code never uses the word 'hazard'. Its nearest concept is the systemic risk source, defined here: a factor that alone or in combination might give rise to systemic risk.
The list of sources (14 capabilities, 10 propensities, 13 affordances and contextual factors) is the closest thing the Code has to a hazard inventory.

catastrophic risk.quote: LEGAL TEXT Article 3(64) AI Act: 'high-impact capabilities' means capabilities that match or exceed
catastrophic risk.note: The Code never uses 'catastrophic'. Its concept is 'systemic risk', defined by AI Act Art. 3(65), quoted here. There is no casualty or monetary threshold anywhere in the Code.
What makes a risk systemic: specific to high-impact capabilities, significant impact on the Union market, propagated at scale.
The four risks every signatory must treat as identified: CBRN, loss of control, cyber offence, harmful manipulation.
The severity-like features: high velocity, cascading, difficult or impossible to reverse, asymmetric impact.
The five types from Art. 3(65), and the examples identification must draw on, including 'risks of major accidents'.

catastrophic risk.quote: Measure 4.1 Systemic risk acceptance criteria and acceptance determination
catastrophic risk.note: Where the thresholds actually come from: each signatory's own systemic risk tiers, capability-defined, which it must justify.

catastrophic risk.note: Appendix 1 is read in light of probability and severity of harm (Art. 3(2)) and Art. 3(65).

loss of control.quote: (2) Loss of control: Risks from humans losing the ability to reliably direct, modify, or shut down a model.
loss of control.note: The definition, a specified systemic risk. 'Humans' is unqualified (not 'the developer'); 'reliably' applies to all three verbs; the second sentence lists origins, not definitional conditions.
The propensities the definition names as origins: misalignment with human intent or values, resistance to goal modification, power-seeking, collusion.
The capability sources: autonomy, self-reasoning (incl. knowing it is evaluated), evading human oversight, self-replication and self-improvement, automating AI R&D.

loss of control.quote: 'insider threats' | hostile operations by humans, AI models, and/or AI systems
loss of control.note: The Glossary makes the model itself a possible insider threat (self-exfiltration), which brings loss of control into the security Commitment.

loss of control.note: Defined behaviourally, including evaluation-aware under-performing and undermining oversight.

what must a developer publish or report.quote: Commitment 7 Safety and Security Model Reports
what must a developer publish or report.note: A Model Report to the AI Office 'before placing a model on the market'. The Code's words are 'Signatory' and 'placing on the market', not 'developer' and 'deploying'.

What the Model Report contains: model description and spec, reasons for proceeding, documentation of assessment and mitigation (including evaluation results and five random samples per evaluation), external reports, landscape changes.
Access 'by the time they place a model on the market'; a delay of up to 15 business days with an interim report.
